summary: Mobility is returning to near‑normal levels (MF‑Index 71) and PT ridership is at about 86% of pre‑pandemic daily volumes, but actual fuel‑saving outcomes remain far below the theoretical ceiling. High‑risk sectors such as Retail, Logistics and Construction continue to drive travel, creating economic exposure despite a strong fuel‑price signal.

signals.detail: The theoretical ceiling of 35.7 M L/week saved is not being realised; only 334 k L were recorded in the first week of the mandate (~1% of the ceiling). High fuel prices (RON95 RM4.27/L) have not translated into measurable savings, indicating weak compliance and limited environmental benefit.

Daily PT trips reached 1.24 M, roughly 86% of the 2019 pre‑pandemic daily average (≈1.43 M). The ridership component of the MF‑Index (72.7) shows steady recovery, though further incentives are needed to close the remaining gap.

Retail & Services, Logistics and Construction exhibit mobility scores above 85 with WFH adoption below 15%, signalling high exposure to congestion, fuel cost volatility and labour productivity losses. These sectors account for the bulk of remaining travel demand.

WFH adoption is uneven: Public & GLCs at 60% versus Construction at 5%. The disparity creates equity concerns, as lower‑wage, high‑mobility workers bear disproportionate travel costs and emissions without comparable policy support.

Elevated fuel prices and a full‑score fuel‑policy component suggest a latent incentive for modal shift, yet low actual fuel savings and modest PT growth temper the shift. Continued price pressure combined with targeted PT subsidies could accelerate a durable transition.

recommendation: Introduce graduated fuel‑tax rebates tied to verified weekly fuel‑saving milestones (target 0.5% of theoretical ceiling by Q2 2027) and expand sector‑specific WFH incentives for Retail, Logistics and Construction. Simultaneously, boost PT attractiveness with fare discounts and service frequency upgrades to achieve 1.5 M daily trips by mid‑2027, while monitoring equity impacts across low‑WFH occupations.
